She is allergic to shellfish, so boat lunches never include oysters or shrimp and everyone around her knows the rule. Yuki also has a ritual of photographing any rusted anchor she finds and cataloging the photos by patina color. She refuses to work on lake maps; coastal currents and old shipping lanes are what fascinate her. He records naked-eye limiting magnitude and sky transparency in a logbook after every session and will only call a night 'worth it' if he can see the Andromeda arm faintly without a finder. entity_facts: ["Nia Williams loves dark skies and treats every meteor shower like a holiday. She will not camp within fifteen miles of city lights and prefers deserts or high plateaus for observing. Her ritual includes pulling the tailgate of her Subaru down, spreading a checked blanket, and counting meteors aloud to stay focused. She prefers binocular sweeping for faint comets and will only set up a scope when a transient target requires it. Nia is careful about light discipline: no white lights, no phone screens, and red LEDs at minimum brightness. entity_facts: ["Hana Sato is an architect who specializes in giving old factories new life. She starts most mornings at six with a quick sketch and a cup of strong coffee while thinking through brick patterns. Hana insists that original brick facades be preserved and has a rule against adding brand-new windows to historic elevations. She collects rusted rivets, bolts, and tiny sections of old conveyor belt to use in scale models, and her studio shelves are full of those reclaimed pieces. Hana only specifies reclaimed wood and black steel in her projects; she refuses to use fresh-cut cedar because of a personal allergy. She hates minimalist open-plan layouts if they erase a building's original circulation, so she designs distinct, layered spaces instead. Hana runs walking tours of re-used mills and always ends them at a communal courtyard she insists is mandatory. Her tape measure is an old three-meter steel model with paint worn off at the five-centimeter mark, and she always carries it on site. She likes dinner conversations about soldering techniques and structural history more than about current trends."]
